messages:
sam: Quick RFC follow-up — proposing a "deferred-ack" pattern for streaming responses at the edge. Edge would ACK receipt of the request and stream partial chunks immediately, but delay the final "commit" until either (a) backend checkpoint confirms persistence or (b) a timeout. Goal: reduce head-of-line blocking when backends stall during long-generation tails. Thoughts?
maya: curious — how does this differ from our current resumable-stream token approach? any protocol changes? @sam
alex: main concern: retries + partial responses = duplicate side effects. if client retries and we re-stream earlier chunks, we might double-execute hooked actions. need idempotency.
sam: good call. high level: no protocol-level change for client streaming. new metadata between edge<->upstream only. edge tracks a "stream-offset" and a soft commit token. rough sketch:
```
edge -> upstream: start(idempotency_token, offset=0)
up -> edge: chunk(offset=0..N, checkpoint_token=ck1)
edge -> client: chunk(s)
...
up -> edge: checkpoint(ck1)  # persisted up to offset N
edge: mark checkpoint as durable, then allow final ACK -> client
```
If client retries with same idempotency_token+offset, upstream can resume from ck1.
jonah: two practical issues: 1) KV cache size — holding uncommitted streams could blow memory for a few bad requests; 2) how long do we wait for checkpoint before expiring stream?
ruth: from an SLO standpoint, delaying final ACK might increase p99 for request completion. we need clear SLO semantics: streaming first byte latency vs final commit latency. who owns the latter?
sam: agree — split SLO: "stream-visible" (first chunk to client) stays low; "commit-complete" can be higher and optional for best-effort workloads. for critical workloads we expose a flag: require_strict_commit=true which blocks final response until checkpoint.
maya: what if upstream never responds to checkpoint (OOM, crash)? fallback plan? degrade gracefully? :thinking:
alex: fallback: if checkpoint not received within X ms, edge stops waiting and returns a `partial-resume-token` to the client so they can reconnect and resume. if resume fails, fall back to degrade-path (serve cached fallback or short-circuit). but this needs to be plumbed into API semantics. clients must understand partial state.
jonah: operationally, we should bound memory by swapping uncommitted chunks to local SSD and enforce per-tenant caps. also preserve in-flight diagnostics: stash trace id + offset to make debugging easier.
ruth: we should also measure the user-visible error modes: how often resume token is required, resume success rate, and p99 commit-latency. add these to per-route dashboards.
deploy-bot: canary created: edge/deferred-ack v1 -> 10% traffic on prod-canary cluster, rollout window 72h. Logs forwarded to infra-telemetry.
alex: recommend an experiment plan: 10% A, 10% B (deferred-ack off), synthetic long tail gen traffic + real production traffic. validate no increase in duplicate side-effects. also run chaos tests where upstream loses checkpoint messages.
jonah: config knobs proposal (example):
```yaml
edge.deferred_ack.enabled: true
edge.deferred_ack.checkpoint_timeout_ms: 15000
edge.deferred_ack.max_uncommitted_bytes_per_tenant: 50MB
edge.deferred_ack.resume_window_secs: 300
edge.deferred_ack.require_strict_commit_flag: false
```
ruth: happy to own dashboards and perf tests. I'll add a gating criterion: resume_success_rate > 99.5% and duplicate_side_effects == 0 (via synthetic hooks) before widening canary. :+1:
sam: thanks — next steps: write short design note (I can draft today), add config knobs to the edge config RFC, and schedule the A/B canary. @alex to lead duplication tests, @ruth for metrics, @jonah for infra limits. I'll post the draft in #architecture-docs when done.
